parsed.explanation: The combined regime creates universal, traveller-facing exposure: division law confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in all public buildings including airports, imposes fines and private bounty suits, and invalidates state IDs with mismatched markers. National border policy lets officers refuse cases with sex discrepancies and consider lifetime fraud findings; existing X passports are time-limited and litigation unresolved. Immigration custody has documented beatings, forced labour, solitary and sexual abuse. National hate-crime coverage, state public-accommodation protection, and pending lawsuits are real but do not enjoin the facility/ID regime. No execution or routine imprisonment for mere identity is documented, but the airport/facility and border exposures are severe and unavoidable for an outed traveller.

entry_documents.exposure: National policy restricts passport sex markers to birth sex, border officers may refuse cases with sex discrepancies, and suspected misrepresentation can support permanent fraud ineligibility. Division law invalidates state IDs inconsistent with birth sex.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; civil-liberties litigation and a legal-aid FAQ challenge or explain the rules, but no ruling enjoins them.
entry_documents.interaction: A foreign passport or ID mismatch can trigger secondary screening at the airport, refusal of entry, or referral into immigration custody, where division facility rules also apply in public airport buildings.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody is documented to include forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of transgender men. Division facility violations carry criminal and civil penalties and private bounty suits.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National hate-crime law covers gender identity and some executive orders have been enjoined, but no operative protection against immigration-custody abuse or the division facility penalties is documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border document discrepancy can move a traveller into immigration detention, where national custody practice governs and division facility/ID rules compound the outing.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Division law confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in publicly owned buildings including airports, schools and government offices; penalties reach $1,000 and any private person may sue for at least $1,000. Existing licences with mismatched markers are invalidated.
federal_state_facilities.protection: State public-accommodation law has covered gender identity since 2020 and a lawsuit was filed within days, but no injunction blocks the facility or ID provisions.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: The airport is both a national border checkpoint and a division public building, so a traveller can face document screening and facility-bounty exposure in the same journey stage.

care_services.exposure: Division law bans gender-affirming care for minors; national policy threatens funding and insurance reimbursement for trans care and custody rules have removed hormone medication from inmates.
care_services.protection: A May 2026 state injunction blocks the minors' care ban in a parental lawsuit; national courts have enjoined some related orders, but adult visitor care access is not documented as protected.
care_services.interaction: A travelling minor needing care faces the division ban and national funding restrictions; an adult relying on medication faces custody denial if detained.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National executive orders and counterterrorism guidance use 'radical gender ideology' and prioritise 'radically pro-transgender' groups; a reward system for reporting domestic-terror leaders creates an official hostile signal.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: National hate-crime law covers gender identity, several orders are in litigation, and the dossier does not document counterterrorism powers being applied to trans visitors.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official threat-framing raises the chance that police or border officials treat visible trans status as suspicious, but the dossier stops short of documented enforcement against visitors.

minors_guardians.exposure: A trans minor visitor is subject to the same division birth-sex facility rules and bounty suits; the division bans gender-affirming care for minors. National policy threatens prosecution of teachers who affirm trans minors, not visitors directly.
minors_guardians.protection: The minors' care ban is under a May 2026 injunction; the facility/ID lawsuit is pending without relief. No visitor-specific guardian protection is documented.
minors_guardians.interaction: A guardian accompanying a trans minor through an airport or public building cannot rely on family status to avoid the facility or ID rules; care access is also restricted.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: The private bounty invites strangers to report or confront trans people in facilities; division hate-crime law omits gender identity, and no trans-specific violence data for visitors is documented.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime law covers gender identity and state public-accommodation law covers gender identity, but police response to bounty-style private enforcement is undocumented.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: A facility encounter can move from social confrontation to a private lawsuit or police call, with national hate-crime coverage available only after an assault is reported.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: The division facility/ID lawsuit is unresolved, no enforcement data on licence invalidations or bounty suits is recorded, and national passport litigation is pending.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-liberties litigation, a legal-aid FAQ, national hate-crime law, and some court injunctions provide partial recourse, but no ruling blocks the core facility/ID or border rules.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies exist mainly after harm and depend on which orders are in force at travel time; the traveller cannot reliably obtain pre-travel clarification or an injunction against the airport facility rule.

anchor_checks.comparison: The 0.35-A regime denies entry and humiliates but does not criminalise facility use or create private bounties. This dossier adds universal birth-sex facility rules in airports, criminal/civil penalties, ID invalidation, private lawsuits, and documented immigration-custody abuse, so it sits materially below 0.35-A.

The 0.25-A regime has police raids, extortion, short jail and no execution, but not a universal private bounty or automatic state-ID invalidation. This dossier's facility bounty and airport/public-building exposure are comparable in severity, while its documented police-raid pattern is thinner, placing it near 0.25-A.

The 0.15-A regime features routine arrests for presentation, months of pretrial custody, beatings and an uncertain capital pathway. This dossier documents severe border and custody harms but not routine arrest for mere presentation or capital exposure, so it is clearly above 0.15-A.

parsed.synthesis: The national and division regimes interact at the airport: document screening can trigger refusal or immigration custody, while the airport is also a division public building where birth-sex facility rules, fines and private bounty suits apply. National hate-crime coverage, state public-accommodation law and pending litigation are real protections, but none is shown to enjoin the facility or ID provisions. The result is a high-risk destination for an outed trans visitor, driven by universal facility/ID exposure and severe border/custody consequences rather than execution or routine imprisonment for identity alone.
